title: Insta-impact: evaluating media forms used by non-profit organizations to engage with their publics on Instagram
abstract: Social media platforms are an important messaging tool for both for-profit and nonprofit organizations, and understanding effective ways to utilize these platforms will help organizations connect with their publics going forward. This study seeks to identify the relationship between the type of media included in posts and the level of audience engagement for non-profit organizations on Instagram. The problem researched was which form of media; photos, videos or mixed media, would have the largest reach when it comes to likes and comments on the platform. This study will collect content, likes and comments for 75 organizations on the platform of Instagram over a weeklong period. The hypothesis states that mixed media postings will show a heightened amount of interaction in comparison to the other media collected. This trend will be seen after the finalization of the data collection and the reaching of conclusions.

title: YouTube Influencers: Are There Too Many Commentary and Reaction Stars in the Spotlight?
abstract: YouTube has permeated the everyday lives of millions of people and created an online entertainment platform where people can create and share video content. Since its beginnings in 2005, it has grown from a simple source of entertainment to a complex ecosystem where popular creators can make a living off of their content. Both large and small YouTubers have the opportunity to follow a successful YouTube career path, and now, creators can be part of a niche subcategory to reach a dedicated fanbase. Being a YouTuber is not always glamorous or fun; often, YouTube creators can become the center of drama in their community, or be faced with stiff competition on a platform filled with other popular creators. Additionally, getting started in a subcategory can be daunting, as there are thousands of channels for watchers to choose from of people making very similar content. Why do people watch more than one creator in a subcategory when those YouTubers often make videos that are either similar in format, content, or both? YouTubers often have strong personalities, a fresh take on popular or old topics, and have other ventures or previous success online that allows them to be prosperous even with many other channels in their subcategory. Using Jake Paul as a boundary-definer, the commentary channels of Kurtis Conner, Danny Gonzalez, and Drew Gooden will act as case studies to identify why people will watch more than one channel in a particular subcategory, even when their content can be very similar.

title: Effective Usage of Instagram as a Food Influencer
abstract: Social media allows individuals to reach publics worldwide within seconds. The risks and benefits of organizations using social media as a tool for promotion has been researched extensively with social networks’ growing popularity. In recent years, individual profiles with large followings have been used as opinion leaders and have earned the term influencer. This research examines the engagement of influencer’s followers, then analyzes the content with the most engagement. A review of literature and examination of data leads to the thesis of: Due to the rise of social media engagement, it is vital to analyze the content of posts and personalities that elicit this high engagement to determine effective strategies for future influencers.  	This content analysis analyzes the top twelve influencers with the Keto Diet as their main focus on Instagram. Posts are collected over a six-week time period starting the first day of the new year. Posts with the highest engagement are evaluated to categorize the content. Three hypotheses guide this research:  H1: The use of photos of meals will increase likes on an influencer’s post.  H2: The use of cooking videos will increase likes on an influencer’s post.  H3: Personal reflection will increase comments on an influencer’s post.   These results will indicate some best practices for food influencers to use to engagement with their audience on Instagram.

title: The Effects of Photo Editing on an Audience's Emotional Response to Photographs
abstract: Images can change the way people feel about what is going on around the world. The Washington Post (2016) reported that most people tend to look at Facebook headlines with the picture attached rather than read articles when it comes to social media. A study done by computer scientists at Columbia University and the French National Institute shows that 59 percent of links on social media have never been clicked. Most people seem to retweet the news without ever reading it (Dewey, 2016).     When it comes to ethical responsibilities of photojournalists, are they guided by rules set forth by their media organizations? Are photojournalists editing their photos to evoke a certain emotion from their audience? If so, why? Are photojournalists manipulating the news with their photo edits? How does photo editing change an audience’s response to a photograph?

title: Monaco: More Than a Gambling Town
abstract: Monaco is a small city-state located on the French Riviera. Monaco is most commonly known for its high standard of living, wealth, and lavish gambling; however, the small city-state is also known for being a tax haven for both residents and foreign businessmen and women. This presentation will discuss the important role Monaco plays in the world economy and how its infrastructure effects Monaco’s economic efficiency. Monaco attracts about seven million people to its small, yet attractive coastline. With more than one billion euros worth of exports each year, Monaco has more to offer than just its luxury hotels and casinos. There will be a focus on the tourism industry, but some of the smaller industries will be introduced to better understand the Monaco’s economic impact on the rest of the world.

title: Analyzing The Bahamas’ Current and Future Tourism Industry
abstract: The foundation of The Bahamas’ economy is rooted in its tourism industry. This presentation will focus on different aspects of The Bahamas’ highly competitive tourism industry such as the major competitors, government regulation, and changes in demand. Topics surrounding the economic systems, political systems, cultural customs, and geographical benefits will also be discussed. For example, The Bahamas’ temperate weather, beautiful beaches, and proximity to the United States allow the tourism industry to thrive. The information presented will further highlight how tourism-dominated countries are affected by the coronavirus (COVID-19) and how governments abroad are relieving and supplementing the hurting industry. The presentation covers the nation’s current tourism market as it reels from COVID-19 and provides clues into how the market will operate in a post-pandemic world.

title: Alcoholic Beverage Industry in Ireland
abstract: Ireland is a country that has developed significantly into one of the world’s top economies over the past century. It ranks top ten in the world in economic freedom, foreign direct investment flows, and GDP per capita. Ireland has a history of making some of the world’s most highly renowned alcoholic beverages, and it has developed into a prosperous industry that the Irish people are proud of. In my presentation, I will discuss how Ireland’s history, culture, political system, and economic system have helped shape their alcoholic beverage industry into what it has become today. This presentation will also analyze the key role that the alcoholic beverage industry has played in Irish tourism and in the agricultural industry that supports brewers, distillers, and winemakers. I will also discuss the key role of the U.S. and other countries who import Irish alcohol, especially whiskey, which makes up close to half of the Irish alcoholic beverage industry.

My presentation will highlight how the expansion of the ICT industry in Singapore has benefited other industries such as manufacturing and financial sectors. Another part of the presentation will cover the background of Singapore, analyze and discuss its cultural values, economic practices, as well as examples of current developments in the country.

title: Anxiety: Environmental and Otherwise
abstract: “Anxiety: Environmental and Otherwise” is a collection of works from different genres and of different lengths. The pieces vary in tone from professional to confessional. Nonfiction sits next to fiction and experimental forms.    The common thread that binds the pieces together is one of personal values.     The heart of the collection is the importance of discovering one’s self and then making the choice to nurture that identity. With all of life’s strangeness and the impossible abundance of experiences, it can be difficult to truly see one’s self. It’s even more difficult to see why any of us are the way that we are. The pieces in this collection examine impacts: how anxiety disorder can affect a person, what people have done to this planet, and what the planet can do to its people. This collection is one girl’s attempt at introspection, all with the hope that something positive will come of it.     “Anxiety: Environmental and Otherwise” grasps for understanding and begs for progress.  It’s a plea, a lament, and a celebration.     This presentation will include a reading and then time for questions/discussion.

title: Anachronistic Zeppelin Adventure: A Short Story
abstract: "Anachronistic Zeppelin Adventure" isa surrealist historical fiction. Set during the Soviet invasion of Berlin, the story follows a stranded American expatriate who boards a zeppelin to escape the city. During his flight, he smokes and dines with two deserters and grapples with his early infatuation with the Nazi regime. Edward rode into Germany on an airship like the one he leaves it on, bewitched by the industry and culture of the country. A historian by trade, he even published some fawning articles about the regime, only realizing he was supporting evil when it was too late.    Like his faith in the Nazis, his grip on reality itself starts to waver. Edward begins to notice inconsistencies with the airship, culminating in his remembering zeppelins haven’t flown for years. The ship disappears, spilling him into the ocean. Waking, he finds himself in his basement in bombed-out Berlin. His fever dream subsides as the Jewish girl, he has been hiding, wipes his head with a cool cloth.

title: Invasive crayfish Faxonius rusticus prefer pheromones of opposite sex conspecifics during the breeding season
abstract: The invasive crayfish Faxonius rusticus has invaded most watersheds in Pennsylvania, spreading throughout the Northeastern United States. Existing methods to regulate F. rusticus populations have been ineffective.  Because crayfish communicate chemically through pheromones, understanding what information these pheromones carry can help improve trapping methods. The aim of this study was to determine how F. rusticus respond to chemical signals produced by same and opposite sex conspecifics during breeding and non-breeding seasons.  Previous studies in our lab have shown that when presented with a choice of either a pheromone or a water control, female F. rusticus are attracted to pheromones produced by males. While males avoid signals of conspecific males, they don’t exhibit a differential response to female signals. In this study, we utilized a Y-maze to present F. rusticus with a choice of male or female conspecific pheromone simultaneously, during breeding and nonbreeding seasons. Crayfish behavior in the Y-maze was videotaped and individuals were believed to make a choice when they moved towards or away from one of the arms. Our findings show that females prefer male pheromones during breeding season, but do not exhibit a preference during non-breeding season. Males entered the arm of the maze with female pheromones more often during the breeding season, but that response was not statistically significant. Both males and females showed a preference for opposite-sex pheromones and avoided same-sex pheromones during the breeding season, but showed no preference for either pheromone during non-breeding seasons.

title: Microbiome Integrity of Unprocessed Canis familiaris Stool Samples Prior to Storage for Fecal Matter Transplants
abstract: Fecal microbiota transplants (FMT) are used for patients with dysbiosis of their gut microbiome or are facing endogenous pathogens. While FMTs are promising, it has become apparent that the gut microbiome varies between individuals and in the same individuals with diet and age. Therefore, it is difficult to establish a microbiome baseline and assess the compatibility of donor stool. A recent approach to address this issue is the storage of stool samples. This storage would prove useful for patients prone to dysbiosis pathologies. The primary goal of this experiment was to analyze changes in the stool microbiome overtime prior to stool sample storage. The alternative hypothesis was that as time passes, endogenous bacteria that are poorly adapted for the external environment would decrease while opportunistic exogenous bacteria would increase. The study was performed with stool samples passively obtained from Canis familiaris. Samples were set out in room temperature for 0 hours, 1 hour, 2 hours, 3 hours, and 2 days. Once the allotted time passed, the samples were homogenized and underwent DNA extraction and PCR amplification of the V4 16S DNA region. Preliminary findings show that there was a substantial change in the microbiome for the samples left out for 2 days. These results suggest that the microbiome does change as time passes prior to processing. Finalized data will assist in understanding the time sensitivity of sample collection and processing along with microbiome integrity, which can guide future practices of stool collection and processing.

title: Comparison of Two Anesthetic Protocols in American Black Bears (Ursus americanus)
abstract: An optimal anesthetic agent should induce rapid immobilization, allow for rapid recovery and have a wide margin of safety. The ketamine and xylazine (KX) drug combination has been commonly used to anesthetize black bears however has been proven unreliable due to inconsistent recovery times and risk the animal for convulsions and hyperthermia due to the high dose of ketamine that is required. The ketamine, xylazine and telazol (TKX) drug combination has not been recorded in black bears. The TKX combination is able to target receptors in the CNS more specifically which could result in a lower dosage required. Exploration of the TKX combination is of interest is combination with the reversal drug, yohimbine, which accelerates recovery through the reversal of sedative effects. To assess the performance of KX and TKX, vital signs, induction times and recovery times were recorded for both protocols. These variables were compared across different metabolic states and statistical analyses were performed using R-Studio. The anesthetic protocols were administered to sixteen American black bears (Ursus americanus) that were captured by the Virginia Department of Game and Inland Fisheries between 2012-2016. Data analyses resulted in more consistent vitals while using the TKX protocol in comparison to the KX protocol. Induction time was greatly affected by status, resulting in inconsistency in the KX and TKX protocol during hibernation and increased induction times during pre/post hibernation. The use yohimbine resulted in quicker recovery to head up and all four. Overall, TKX resulted in more consistent measurements compared to KX.

title: The effect of poly(I:C) on the immune system as observed through IL-12 production in dendritic cells
abstract: Activation of dendritic cells (DCs) through chemical treatment causes release of cytokines. Original studies demonstrated that MuTu DCs, derived from the spleen of mice, responded to stimulation of TLR3 with poly(I:C) by producing IL-12. Challenges in culture of MuTu DCs led to the transition to culture of the DC2.4 cell line. DC2.4 cells are also murine dendritic cells but derived from the bone marrow. Both DC lines express TLR3. To compare the response of DC2.4 cells to MuTu DCs, studies using varying doses and times of poly(I:C) exposure were conducted. In contrast to MuTu DCs, DC2.4 cells produced little to no IL-12 after 12-hour exposure to doses less than 5 µg/mL poly(I:C). Additional experiments determined what dose of poly(I:C) and exposure time was required to stimulate DC2.4 to produce larger amounts of IL-12. Other ongoing studies are investigating whether corticosterone (CORT) alters IL-12 production by DC2.4. CORT is a stress hormone known to suppress IL-12 production by MuTu DCs. Following activation, DCs often undergo programmed cell death, or apoptosis. This occurred when MuTu DCs were stimulated with poly(I:C). Bim, a member of the Bcl-2 family of proteins, promotes apoptosis, which can be triggered through administration of chemicals such as poly(I:C). Bim was successfully detected in Human Diploid Fibroblasts (HDF), which will serve as a positive control to optimize Bim detection in DCs. Analysis of the production of IL-12 by DCs and their subsequent apoptosis allows for greater understanding of how stress-induced chemicals affect our ability to fight pathogens.

title: Desalination
abstract: Our team aims to solve the issue of short-term freshwater shortages in coastal disaster-relief environments caused by natural disasters through the design of a small-scale portable desalination unit. Our project has two potential phases: first, we research, design, and build a smaller, tabletop unit capable of exploiting our chosen method of desalination: electrodialysis. Then, we aim to use the information from tuning and testing this unit, to design the full-size, truck bed-mounted unit. We chose desalination by electrodialysis because of its simplicity and low-power requirement compared to reverse osmosis. Our design includes a stack of select ion-permeable membranes in an electrically charged tank with corresponding valving for supply, clean, and brine solutions. The tabletop unit will be able to produce desalinated water at 3.34L/h from typical seawater concentration, and the full-size unit will be able to produce more practical amounts capable of sustaining a small group of individuals. For SCAD, we will have the small-scale unit fabricated and functioning.

title: Elizabethtown Surrey Performance Testing and Mechanical Simulation
abstract: The Elizabethtown College owned Surrey Bike has served as a platform for engineering projects for several years and has undergone various improvements. The most recent upgrades to the disassembled Surrey from last spring include a full body restoration and the addition of an electric wheel assist. A final reassembly and testing phase was intended, but never completed. Our mission was to follow through with this reassembly and testing phase, and then take it a step further. The project scope includes a reassembly of the Surrey bike, performance tests, and a computer simulation modeling the mechanical system. Reassembly will happen in the college fabrication lab and be based on updated fabrication specifications. Performance testing will occur on a quarter mile loop circling Brinser field which includes various hill grades. Power and work will be calculated after recording the system’s weight and speed on certain hill grades during multiple trials of performance testing. Resistance forces will be accounted for as accurately as possible depending on the available resources. The mechanical system will be modeled in Simbody with previously recorded performance metrics serving as inputs. We hope the simulation can be used by future groups as a tool to inspire further Surrey upgrades

title: Automated Hydroponics System
abstract: Climate change is an issue that has inspired modern engineers and scientists to find new ways to maintain our lifestyle without harming the environment. Our group has worked on building an automated hydroponics system using the deep-water culture method to grow kale and lettuce. Our hydroponics system is expected to use less space and fewer resources than those used in regular farming practices to grow equivalent crop yields. In terms of automation, the system will be able to detect when some of the factors that guarantee its optimal performance (pH level, amount of nutrients in solution, etc.) are not what they need to be and will notify a Dining Services employee so that they can remedy the issue. Dining Services would benefit by gaining the ability to grow their own vegetables and save food expenses if the system keeps operating. The engineering and biology departments would also benefit by having another project to experiment with and gain experience in a field that will become more relevant in the coming years.

title: Portable Hydro-Generator
abstract: The problem that is being addressed is the lack of lightweight and affordable clean energy sources to charge various small devices for those in remote locations such as on a backpacking trip. Our team is addressing this issue by designing a compartment housing multiple generators and a series of electrical components that will convert power from running water into electrical energy. This assembly must be fully waterproof and able to withstand the punishment that comes with being placed in natural water sources as well as a backpack during long hours of hiking. Whether this means high current in the water, erosion from sediment, or tight packing, the system will have to endure. The team will have a working prototype for SCAD, which will demonstrate how the generator functions, its durability, and the time it takes to fully charge a standard IPhone. This will show the effectiveness of the generator and provide a proof of concept for the design.

title: Parking Spot Sensor
abstract: One of the biggest problems in large cities is trying to find an open parking spot. Drivers spend extra time circling blocks or otherwise searching for available spots, creating additional carbon emissions. This can also cause unnecessary frustration which creates the potential for more reckless or aggressive driving. We believe our sensor design that can monitor parking availability and transmit that information in real-time to an easily accessible web interface will solve this problem. In theory, installed on the ground of parking spots throughout a city, the parking spot sensor will detect the presence of cars parked above it. For SCAD, we will have a functional prototype consisting of a solar panel, ultrasonic sensor, and Arduino in a waterproof housing. We will test our prototype to ensure optimal performance and reasonable data transmission speed. In addition to our prototype, we will model our final housing design using Inventor with improvements made based on insufficiencies in durability and waterproofing in our prototype to better suit the needs of the urban environment in which the model would exist.

title: Power Assisted Stretcher
abstract: Due to the current public health situation involving COVID-19 and an influx of patients admitted into hospitals, there are rising concerns about the safe and efficient transport of incapacitated patients. Nurses, EMTs, and medical personnel commonly struggle to push manual stretchers occupied by patients and medical equipment; this causes increased rates of work-related injuries, subsequently leading to unsafe patient-transport. Our group is designing and fabricating a prototypical, push-power-assisted stretcher to replace the need for manual stretchers in hospitals, ambulances, and care facilities. We are assembling the electrical and mechanical components of the stretcher onto a shopping cart. The shopping cart will prevent us from accidentally compromising the structural integrity of the medical stretcher received as a donation. After fabrication, cyclic loading and testing will provide a portfolio of product deliverables to future project groups. Future project groups will modify and apply our prototype to the medical stretcher model for a final product. We will have a completed prototype with testing data at SCAD.

title: RC Research Boat
abstract: Continuous improvement of the curriculum and student success rates requires enhanced opportunities, systems, and interdepartmental collaboration. These demands require an unprecedented and generational device tailored to the needs of successful student research. This new device must attract future generations of Blue Jays in both the Biology and Engineering Departments while providing a source for continued learning, service, and sustainability. Nearly one year of technical design, analysis, and fabrication resulted in the creation of a portable remote-controlled research boat. Preliminary testing and use in Lake Placida will expose students to the characteristics of their campus environment and elevate the visibility of the institution's renowned programs. Dual electric motors provide consistent power and smooth steering while minimizing the threat to aquatic life or damage from submerged objects. The boat enables measurement of water temperature and pH and establishes a platform for future development and customization of its equipment. SCAD 2021 presents the opportunity to exhibit a functional proof of concept capable of fulfilling research and marketing demands while also satisfying the requirements for EGR402: Senior Project in Engineering II.

title: Stronger Together: A Service Project
abstract: Our group, Team Stronger Together, is part of the SDLC program on campus at Elizabethtown College. In the 2020-2021 academic year, we had the opportunity to work alongside Mom’s House of Lancaster. Mom’s House is a non-profit organization that helps single mothers return to school while providing free childcare and educational services to the mothers. Since SDLC projects were changed to remote this academic year, our group had to collaborate on project approaches that would best benefit Mom’s House, while taking place on an online platform. In the fall semester, our group created a gift card drive, that benefited the mothers during the holiday season. This allowed the moms to have financial support during a stressful season, but still allowed them the independence to use the gift cards however it benefited them the most. The gift card drive was an overall success. After seeing the results from the fall semester, we wanted to recreate a drive that would continue to benefit Mom’s House as an organization as well as the moms who utilize the services. In the spring semester, we created a school supply drive. This drive consists of materials that are in demand at Mom’s House, benefitting the organization, the moms, and the children. The drive will take place throughout April, having the materials delivered to Mom’s House by May. We are still awaiting results as to the success of this drive, but we are hopeful for results similar to the fall semester.

title: Helping Hands: A Service Project
abstract: Much like the other groups, COVID-19 has forced us to pivot from our original plan. In speaking with our community partner with Caitlin’s Smiles, Skip Wachter, we asked them what would be of the most assistance to their organization during these trying times, as well as in the future. Our initial conversation resulted in the idea of our group creating “pick-me-up cards” for children with lengthy stays in the hospital, along with those who have siblings or family members with lengthy stays in the hospital as well. These cards involved a colorful and childish picture, typically of a cartoon character or a Disney character on the front, with a fun quote or quick little joke on the inside pertaining to the picture on the front, with the hopes of putting a smile on the child’s face and taking their mind off of the current situation that they are in. Mr. Wachter informed us that these cards are an essential part of their “bags of smiles.” By the end of the first semester, we were able to provide Caitlin’s Smiles with approximately 200 cards that were guaranteed to provide smiles on the faces of children. When we went to drop off the cards, Mr. Wachter was very generous and provided us with a tour of his facilities. Upon completing the tour, it motivated us to want to continue to be involved with the organization beyond our tenure at Elizabethtown College. While we offered to provide a different service for the spring semester, Mr. Wachter once again pushed for our involvement to be primarily with the “pick-me up cards.” Knowing how long it took to produce 200 cards in the first semester, our goal for the second semester is to at least match that amount. In a normal year, we would have loved to personally deliver these cards to the kids in the hospital, but our involvement for the time being will have to remain at a distance.

title: How Community-based Nutrition Education Impacts Health Disparities Among Black American Adolescents.
abstract: Although the United States (US) has substantially increased medical technology and health care advancements, a growing disparity concerning health literacy and health outcomes exists compared to peer countries (Palloni & Yonker, 2015). These health disparities exist particularly among racial minorities (Kinsella & Durocher, 2016). Consequently, the US spends millions to investigate the underlying causes to alleviate these health disparities (Amuta-Jimenez et al., 2020). These efforts, however, demonstrate little change with interventions showing limited carry over of learned principles improving individual health, specifically concerning diet or food literacy (Doustmohammadian et al., 2020). Food literacy refers to an individual’s nutrition knowledge and food skills which influence food choices, impacting overall health and well being (Cullen et al., 2015). Food literacy specifically falls into two occupations, eating and meal preparation, as categorized by the Occupational Therapy Practice Framework (American Occupational Therapy Association (AOTA), 2020).   Nutritious food intake during adolescence is critical for growth, maintenance of physical health, and development of healthy weight (Brooks & Begley, 2013). As a result of decreased food literacy, Black adolescents may experience occupational injustice related to occupations of eating, meal preparation, and health management and maintenance, resulting in overall decreased health and well-being (Manganello & Sojka, 2016). The literature suggests there is a gap in knowledge in how to increase healthy food consumption among Black adolescents and a gap in research regarding successful food literacy interventions for Black adolescents. A scoping review was conducted to understand the availability of community-based nutrition education programs that are available to Black adolescents.
requested_duration: Poster

title: Occupational Therapists' Perspectives on Working in Mental Health Roles
abstract: Occupational therapists working in mental health settings face a multitude of challenges to practice, including role blurring, generic roles, lack of support, and a lack of community, yet continue to pursue these positions. The current literature primarily highlights these barriers and discusses the under utilization of occupational therapists in this area. Despite these challenges, occupational therapists are still holding prominent roles in mental health and the question remains of how these therapists are creating meaning from these roles and what is facilitating their success. For this research, I conducted interviews with occupational therapists in order to gain a better understanding of the occupational therapists’ perspectives of their role in mental health. Qualitative analysis of  the results will provide insights into what can be done to support this role for occupational therapists.
requested_duration: Poster

title: Post-Intensive Care Syndrome: Current Practice and Knowledge
abstract: Post-Intensive Care Syndrome (PICS) is an broad diagnosis that encompasses a variety of cognitive, physical, and psychological impairments that may be experienced by individuals who have been admitted to the Intensive Care Unit (ICU). This phenomena results in functional declines (Activities of daily living/Instrumental activities of daily living) and economic distress. The literature suggests few interventions for this population and related implications. However, according to the literature, there is a clear underutilization of Occupational Therapy services for both the cognitive and psychological components of PICS. Additionally, there is a lack of consistency regarding assessments and evaluations used with this population. These factors have contributed to the absence of a standard, or model of care to guide the Occupational Therapy process with individuals at risk for and suffering from PICS. The purpose of this study is to create a better understanding of Occupational Therapists’ current knowledge and practice behaviors regarding this Post-Intensive Care Syndrome. This project was completed via a mixed methods survey of occupational therapists in PA. Final conclusions/results will be shared in full at SCAD.
requested_duration: Poster

title: Unusually Cruel: Death Penalty Sentencing & Mentally Ill Offenders
abstract: Application of the death penalty has long been a controversial piece of the United States criminal justice system, particularly when this punishment is applied to those suffering from severe mental illness. This research seeks to explain how the Eighth Amendment should protect those with mental illness from receiving the death penalty as a punishment. The intricate connection between psychology and the law will be detailed throughout this research as well. Furthermore, this research examines case law at both the Federal and Pennsylvania state level relevant to who the death penalty may apply to, as well as how those with mental illnesses are to be treated and viewed by courts. Review of this case law includes the review of the eligibility of a mentally ill defendant to assert a diminished capacity defense or “not guilty by reason of insanity” (NGRI) plea. This research also delves into the impacts federalism and expert testimony have on the likelihood the Court and the jury will accept these defenses or pleas. This research concludes with a synthesis of solutions to these seemingly insurmountable issues within the system.
requested_duration: Poster

title: Therapists’ Perspectives on Using Telehealth with Spinal Cord Injury Patients
abstract: The purpose of this study and presentation is to understand/explain the perspectives of occupational therapists in using telehealth with spinal cord injury (SCI) patients. Patients with SCI benefit from telehealth since it provides increased accessibility to needed rehabilitation services that are not otherwise available. Although telehealth has been used for many years with this population, COVID-19 has caused many traditional in-person rehabilitation services to quickly switch to telehealth for the first time.          People with SCI require continued, long-term outpatient rehabilitation after discharge from acute care rehabilitation hospitals. Unfortunately, they often lose access to the inpatient care team upon discharge home due to the geographic distance combined with their decreased mobility, and now COVID-19. Telehealth can help alleviate this.           However, most previous studies have only focused on SCI patients' experiences and/or perspectives regarding telehealth, or they have solely focused on the use of telehealth with SCI patients in general. Therefore, there is a need to understand the perspectives of the occupational therapists delivering telehealth to this population. This study aims to identify what aspects of delivering telehealth to SCI patients are beneficial and what aspects create challenges for the therapist. The results can help in understanding the challenges and benefits that occupational therapists face when delivering telehealth to SCI patients, which can represent how telehealth sessions are working for these patients and how therapists can most effectively deliver telehealth to this population while also limiting burdens to themselves. The study results are not completed yet, but will be disclosed once finished.
requested_duration: 15 minutes to present, 5 minutes for Q&A

title: Exploring the Use of Occupational Therapy Telehealth Services in Early Intervention During COVID-19
abstract: During COVID-19, many services transitioned to virtual platforms, including occupational therapy (OT) services provided in early intervention (EI) settings, with many service providers and patients thrust into this service delivery model despite limited past experience with it (Neece et al., 2020). While there is preliminary research regarding the effectiveness and benefits of telehealth services in EI OT, there are few rigorous studies comparing telehealth to traditional in-person services (Ashburner et al., 2016; Campbell et al., 2019; Cason, 2009; Gardner et al., 2016; Jacobs et al., 2015; Rortvedt & Jacobs, 2019; Serwe, 2018; Wallisch et al., 2019). Further, given the current nature of COVID-19, there is minimal information from research studies about the imposed transition to telehealth during this time.   The purpose of this research study is to gain an understanding of the use of telehealth in EI OT services during COVID-19 as compared to experiences with previous in-person services from the perspective of OTs and patient families, with a focus on their perspectives about the effectiveness of telehealth during COVID-19, as well as aspects of telehealth services that were beneficial and presented as barriers to its success.  Data for this project is being obtained through semi-structured interviews with EI OTs and families in order to gain an in-depth understanding of their experiences with telehealth during COVID-19, as compared to previous in-person services. Qualitative thematic content analysis (Braun & Clarke, 2006) will be used to analyze the data. Results from this study will be shared in a presentation session at SCAD.
requested_duration: 15 minutes to present, 5 minutes for Q&A

title: Parents’ Perspectives and Pediatric Constraint Induced Movement Therapy for Children with Cerebral Palsy
abstract: Constraint-induced movement therapy (CIMT) is a treatment used to improve upper extremity functioning for populations experiencing hemiplegia, or unilateral weakness. Constraint-Induced Movement Therapy has been used and shown to be effective for children with hemiplegic cerebral palsy (CP). Constraint-Induced Movement Therapy involves the constraint of the individual’s unaffected extremity along with intensive and shaped repetitive therapeutic activities to enhance overall functional use of the affected extremity. Because this type of therapy is intensive and often results in frustration and other negative reactions from the child, therapists are often hesitant to use it, and parents often experience increased time and effort demands along with worry about the impacts on the child’s behavior. Despite these associated struggles, parents still see the benefits of this type of therapy and report that it is worthwhile. The purpose of this study was to further explore caregiver’s perceptions of CIMT to treat their children with CP. It also aimed to address aspects of the perspectives of caregivers on the family-centered care provided by the therapists. This research study included qualitative thematic analysis of interviews with one or more parents and caregivers of children with hemiplegic CP who received CIMT. Results from this study will be presented and discussed at SCAD.
requested_duration: 15 minutes to present, 5 minutes for Q&A

title: Exploring Employment Experiences from the Perspective of Adults with Autism Spectrum Disorder
abstract: Autism Spectrum Disorder, commonly referred to as ASD or autism, is a neurological disorder defined in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual 5th edition. Persistent deficits in social communication and social interaction across multiple contexts, as well as restricted, repetitive patterns of behavior, interests, or activities are included in the diagnostic criteria. Despite commonalities in symptoms, ASD is a spectrum, meaning that each individual experiences autism differently.  Individuals with ASD face disproportionately high levels of unemployment and underemployment. Engagement in work is often a vital part of an individual’s wellbeing that can help shape their identity. Participation in work can cultivate a sense of purpose. Workplace participation can positively impact different areas of life including social connections, independence, and quality of life.  There are facilitators and barriers to employment that have been identified that generally hold true; however, because ASD presents as a spectrum each individual may have a different story. Currently, the literature has an array of helpful information from different perspectives from key employment stakeholders, including parents, employers, and co-workers; however, there is a lack of detailed firsthand perspectives describing the work experiences of those with ASD. Giving the ASD community a voice and listening to their unique experiences can help raise awareness of their capabilities and provide valuable insight into a key stakeholder perspective that has often been overlooked.
requested_duration: 15 minutes to present, 5 minutes for Q&A

title: Fine Arts Integration in Early Childhood Education
abstract: This study seeks to define fine arts place in all classrooms regardless of subject. This research will explore how fine arts can enhance a lesson or a student’s learning experience and the perceived effects of art integration on students and teachers. Research methodology will include conducting interviews with practicing teachers in both general and special area education to understand their perspectives on fine arts integration.
requested_duration: 15 minutes to present, 5 minutes for Q&A

title: UNDERSTANDING MATH ANXIETY; A STUDY OF PRESERVICE TEACHERSCONFIDENCE AND TEACHING PRACTICES TO LIMIT MATH ANXIETY
abstract: “Mathematics anxiety can be defined as a feeling of tension, apprehension, or even dread that interferes with the ordinary manipulation of numbers and the solving of mathematical problems”(Ashcraft & Faust, 1994, p 98). The physical symptoms of math anxiety include but are not limited to: “heart races; irregular breathing; sweatiness; shakiness; biting nails; feeling of hollowness in stomach; sick to one’s stomach” (Finlayson, 2014, p 105). However, math anxiety can also lead to mental effects such as depression (Peters Mayer, 2008). There are a wide range of causes such as telling students math is easy or that math can be solved in one way as well as a sense of competition in mathematics, math tests, and math anxiety within pre-service teachers(Finlayson, 2014). Within this paper, the aim within the research is to uncover if there is a correlation between pre-service teacher’s math anxiety and their lack of confidence to teach math as well as student’s who identify with math anxiety and specific teaching strategies.
requested_duration: 15 minutes to present, 5 minutes for Q&A

title: Implementing Waldorf-Inspired Practices in Early Childhood Public Education
abstract: Waldorf Education is an alternative approach to schooling that focuses on the intentional practice of educating the whole child ‘head, heart, and hands’. There’s been a recent movement to take aspects of the Waldorf Model and integrate them in public schools. Although there are varying “best practices” for implementing these approaches, more information is needed for the process of integrating these methods into a traditional public school learning environment. The purpose of this study is to investigate strategies that early childhood educators can engage with to inform their pedagogical practices influenced by Waldorf principles. This qualitative study will employ open-ended, semi-structured interview protocol to identify integration barriers and how to do it. I will conduct 30-45 minute Skype interviews with approximately six public-inspired Waldorf school educators who are currently in the field in a variety of schools spanning across the country. The purposeful sample will be drawn from teachers listed on the Public Alliance for Waldorf Education’s website (http://www.allianceforpublicwaldorfeducation.org). Participants must be current Waldorf educators and represent a variety of early childhood grade levels. I will email potential participants describing the purpose of my study. Themes emerging from the interviews will be analyzed to identify common themes among participant responses. Findings will be analyzed to determine the challenges these teachers faced and the methods utilized to accomplish this outcome.
requested_duration: 15 minutes to present, 5 minutes for Q&A

title: “The Trial of Memory Fairchild” - Creating a Fiction Podcast
abstract: Memory Fairchild, an anxious medical student, is put on trial for necromancy when she accidentally kills a patient and brings them back to life.     “The Trial of Memory Fairchild” is an original audio drama podcast that takes place in a modern-magical world and tells the story of a girl trying to figure out what her purpose is, how she can best help the people around her, and what she’s willing to sacrifice.    In the past several years, usage of podcasts as a medium for fiction has expanded. Working with audio to tell stories brings its own joys and challenges, from writing the scripts to creating the sound effects and more. This project consisted of the first season of the podcast, with three episodes lasting roughly 20 minutes long. In addition, the podcast features Elizabethtown College students and alumni as the cast.     As part of the presentation, a small clip of the podcast will be played.
requested_duration: 15 minutes to present, 5 minutes for Q&A

title: Understanding Portrayals of Hunters Across the Media
abstract: Contemporary society possesses a stereotype of hunters that is constructed by mass media reporting and entertainment programming. Following World War II roughly a quarter of American males identified as hunters (Rinella, 2018). Today, hunters represent under 12 million people in the United States, about 4% of the general population (Krebs, 2019). Responsible for nearly $24 billion annually from general hunting purchases and over $3 billion in local, state, and federal tax revenue, American hunters remain a driving force in the national economy despite falling participation (Whitesel, 2017). Through a content analysis of mass media programming, this project will provide a description of how the hunting and outdoor life community is being presented to the public and how those perceptions are changing over time.
requested_duration: 15 minutes to present, 5 minutes for Q&A

title: Norway’s Hydropower
abstract: Norway is the second largest oil and gas producer in the world, next to the middle eastern countries. About one half of Norway’s exports and 20 percent of national GDP come from this industry. In order to reduce its carbon footprint, a total 96 percent of power in Norway comes from hydropower. This presentation will focus on Norwegian hydropower’s sustainable outlook, and what social, political, and economic conditions have led to the integration of hydropower into the grid. More importantly, a focus of the presentation will be on the environmental and economic benefits of sustainable energy in the developed nations to meet the consumer demands with a growing worldwide population.
requested_duration: 15 minutes to present, 5 minutes for Q&A

title: Designer Glass & Shades - A Family Business Case Study
abstract: The paper presents the story of an actual family business, developed as a case study with recommendations and creative solutions. The research is aimed to describe and assess the company, identify the most important challenges faced by the family firm, and develop recommendations on how to solve these issues. Moreover, the paper identifies and discusses two or three growth opportunities of the investigated family business. As methodology, the analysis of the firm is performed according to the three-circle model of the family business system (family, business, and ownership). The paper involves both primary research - in-depth interviews with family members, managers, and owners and other data collection methods, and secondary research - literature review and industry reports.
requested_duration: 15 minutes to present, 5 minutes for Q&A
presenters: Kayla  Patone | Madison Stoyer | Alexandra Sharp | Alyssa  Scordo

title: The Impact of COVID-19 on Job-Search Behavior Among College Students
abstract: The coronavirus pandemic impacted everyone around the globe, and it has disrupted traditional employment processes for college students. This study seeks to identify patterns in college students’ job-search behavior and relevant personality and emotional traits that may influence their job search outcomes during the pandemic. The study expands on current academic theories on personality traits and proactive behaviors in the context of preparatory and active job search processes. Through surveys of Elizabethtown College students, I hope to understand the impact COVID-19 had on students' job-search experiences and the role that psychographic attributes such as emotional intelligence and pandemic anxiety levels played in their job search success.
requested_duration: 15 minutes to present, 5 minutes for Q&A

title: Corporate Social Responsibility in Professional Sports: Perceptions and Demographics
abstract: In America, businesses are looking for ways to truly connect with their customers and key publics. This concept is especially prevalent in sports organizations such as the National Football League (NFL), Major League Baseball (MLB), the National Basketball Association (NBA), and professional tennis. These leagues utilize corporate social responsibility (CSR) messaging to encourage engagement both in the stadium and at home, all the while trying to promote something everyone can enjoy. But, how effective are these tactics? Does utilizing these messaging strategies correlate with increased positivity and greater engagement? There has been some research done into the sociology of sports, which discusses why sports organizations are believed to carry so much weight. The purpose of this research is to determine if certain types of CSR messaging will resonate differently with various demographic groups. A survey was conducted where change in attitude about a sports team was measured. Respondents were asked a series of questions about a sports team. They were then shown a series of CSR promotions that team was developing. Upon seeing those promotions, they were asked the same survey questions. The goal was to determine if the CSR messaging influenced participants’ likelihood to watch the sports team. Business owners and social media professionals can benefit from this study because it gives them insight into consumer preferences and what types of messaging motivates consumers to continue engaging with a certain business or team. This knowledge could aid in guiding businesses decisions especially with consumer engagement.
requested_duration: 15 minutes to present, 5 minutes for Q&A

title: “You have fixed my life- however short,”- Wilfred Owen’s Homosexuality in His Poetry and Prose
abstract: Famed World War One poet Wilfred Owen is perhaps best known for his poems that provide insight into the minds of men who suffered from PTSD, or “shell shock,” caused by fighting in the Great War.  Owen, along with being an incredible poet, was likely a gay man, but many critics have glossed over these unproven aspects of his history for myriad reasons.  While the sexuality of Wilfred Owen cannot be posthumously confirmed, the evidence pointing away from heterosexuality cannot be ignored.  Several of his poems support this idea, namely a few unfinished snippets from his youth and “Greater Love,” a World War One poem with vivid homoerotic imagery.  His sexuality also bleeds through many letters of his, most of them written to his probable lover Siegfried Sassoon.  Owen died tragically young, leaving critics with little writing and life experience to extrapolate from.  However, his relationships and writings make it clear that his feelings toward his fellow soldiers surpassed camaraderie.
requested_duration: 15 minutes to present, 5 minutes for Q&A

title: World War I and Mental Illness in Toni Morrison’s Sula
abstract: Toni Morrison’s Sula is set in the African American community of Medallion during the late-1910s to the mid-1960s. Several of the novel’s characters display apparent mental illnesses. In 2020, I explored this topic in an essay for Dr. Adams’s 400-level English course. I tried my hand at diagnosing several characters. Two of these individuals, Shadrack and Plum, were veterans of the First World War. I plan to focus on these two during my presentation.         I analyzed characters thusly. First, I cross-referenced the DSM-5 with the text of Sula and selected likely ailment(s) supported by shown symptoms. Then, I researched these afflictions to provide historical context for how someone suffering them during novel’s time setting would be perceived by society. Because Morrison’s novel takes place over an extended period, these perceptions are not static but evolve. These broader societal shifts are mirrored in the text by the town’s changing perception of mentally ill characters.  For example, between World War I and II, the public became more understanding of PTSD. The character Shadrack, a victim of PTSD, is initially shunned by the townspeople for his strange behavior. Very gradually, his fellow citizens warm to him, even throwing a parade to celebrate his imaginary holiday. Conversely, Plum, a heroin addict, does not survive his family’s intolerance.       I hope my analyses of Morrison’s characters may offer some insight into the complicated meeting place of the Great War, mental illness, society, and literature.
requested_duration: 15 minutes to present, 5 minutes for Q&A
presenters: Jake Guiswite | Emily Erdlen | Doris Hall
panel_title: World War One in British and American Literature

title: "The Song of the Mud"
abstract: During World War I, Mary Borden published an elaborate and chilling poem called “The Song of the Mud.”  Borden was a suffragist in her late twenties when she began writing about her experience witnessing the war.  An American married to a Briton, she worked as a nurse for the French Red Cross, setting up a field hospital for French soldiers.  Borden had a prime view of the action on the battlefield and the carnage of soldiers following each attack. The poems she wrote were reactions to these events, and her passionate, unfiltered honesty about the front lines would serve to shock and unsettle the families of soldiers back home. In “The Song of the Mud,” she uses the mud as a symbol for the true hostility and inescapable nature of the war zone that British censorship often tried to mask. Throughout her poem, the meaning of the mud is changed and manipulated to highlight different aspects of the trenches, and even to make a mockery of the censorship-borne misconceptions of the British. Front lines were often described as deceptively beautiful, and the poem exemplifies this:  “The pale yellow glistening mud that covers the hills like satin; / The grey gleaming silvery mud that is spread like enamel over the valleys.” The beautiful landscape of Dunkirk hides the dark secrets and horrors of trench warfare and the true hostility and inescapable nature of the war zone.

title: Correlation of BCL-X isoform with Aggressive Growth Rates of SV40 T-antigen Transformed Human Diploid Fibroblasts
abstract: The BCL-2 protein-family are regulators of programed cell death, or apoptosis. Apoptosis is a coordinated set of biochemical reactions that aid in growth and development. Regulatory proteins interact with inhibitors of apoptosis, while others interact with inducers. BCL-X is a specific protein whose mRNA can be spliced to produce products that are either anti-apoptotic (the long form, BCL-XL) or pro-apoptotic (the short form, BCL-Xs). The control of the isoform selection has been ascribed to the splicing factor SAM68.  Our lab is investigating the phenomena that when immortalized-human diploid fibroblasts (HDF(tert)) are transformed with the viral oncoprotein SV40 T-antigen (HDF(tert)+T), the level of SAM68 increases dramatically. To determine if this increased accumulation is correlated to the aggressive growth characteristics, we questioned whether the BCL-X isoform selection was altered. Since BCL-XL has been found to be overexpressed in some human cancers, it was hypothesized that the increase in SAM68 caused by T-antigen would consequently cause an increase in BCL-XL levels. RTPCR was used to compare the BCL-X isoforms in HDF(tert) and HDF(tert)+T cells. Surprisingly, RTPCR data shows that the transformed cells with increased SAM68 protein show no quantitative difference in the BCL-XL to BCL-Xs isoform ratios. Since it has been reported that BCL-XL can accumulate in the cytoplasm, mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum and nuclear margins, immunofluorescence is currently underway to determine if there are cellular location alterations in the virally-transformed cells. If no differences are found, then it can be concluded that SAM68 does not affect cellular growth via BCL-X expression or location.
requested_duration: 15 minutes to present, 5 minutes for Q&A

title: Effect of SV40 T-antigen Oncoprotein Expression in Human Diploid Fibroblasts on the production of SAM68 and subsequent Cyclin D1 Isoform Selection
abstract: Virally induced tumorigenesis accounts for 20% of cancers, totaling 2.8 million new cases yearly. To study viral oncoprotein disruptions, our laboratory employs the simian virus 40 (SV40) T-antigen to induce cellular transformation. In this study, immortalized-human diploid fibroblast cells were transformed with the T-antigen gene.  It was found that the level of the alternative splicing factor, SAM68, increased dramatically in the presence of the oncoprotein. SAM68 RNA-binding protein functions as a splicer, vital to cell proliferation and regulation. This investigation sought to determine if this increased SAM68 was the variant that excludes the KH region (SAMdeltaKH) and does not exhibit splicing activity; or, if the wild-type isoform was amplified.  To determine if the splicing activity was affected, the downstream target cyclin D was assessed. Cyclin D is an early G1 cell cycle regulator, following cellular division. Two cyclin D isoforms (D1a, D1b) have been correlated to various forms of cancer; thus, it was hypothesized that the viral oncoprotein induced high levels of SAM68 which in-turn created a more active cyclin D, promoting the cell cycle. Literature has shown that increased SAM68 in tumor cells select for the non-spliced variant, and thus similar results are expected. Cyclin D isoform selection following SAM68-induced splicing is yet to be determined in T-antigen expressing cell lines, however other studies have shown D1b variant selection in tumor cells. These studies are essential for viral-induced cancer research due to their insight on preferential splicing behavior, and the resulting impact on downstream proteins involved in oncogenesis.
requested_duration: 10 minutes to present, 5 minutes for Q&A

title: Effect of Diquat Dibromide on Hydra Reflex, Tentacle Length and Viability
abstract: Diquat dibromide (DD) is widely used in the US as an algicide and herbicide targeting broadleaf and grassy weeds.  DD works by causing calcium dysregulation in cells leading to an increase in ATP production in mitochondria, leading to ROS accumulation causing oxidative stress and signaled apoptosis. The use of DD has recently been suspended in the EU; thus, experiments were undertaken to investigate its toxicity using Hydra as a model organism. It was hypothesized that DD calcium dysregulation, will result in degeneration of tentacles and nerves of Hydra leading to decreasing feeding behavior, poke-response and viability. Three hydras were placed into triplicate wells containing 0, 0.025, 0.05, 0.1, or 0.5µg/mL of DD, and two species of Hydra, oligatus and vulgaris, were used. For both species, tentacle length showed a statistical decline at all concentrations. After 2-4 days of exposure to DD, both species exhibited a statistically significant diminished poke and feeding response at all concentrations, eventually leading to the absence of response on day 5. It was found that animals in concentrations 0.025, 0.5, 0.1 and 0.05 µg/mL, experienced steady progression of degradation eventually leading to death. The overall hydra viability was also significantly affected at 0.05, 0.1 and 0.5 µg/mL concentrations, although for 0.025µg/mL, overall hydra viability was extending a day longer. These results show evidence of diquat dibromide causing cellular stress leading to tentacle loss, reduction in feeding response, slower poke reactions, and death in both hydra species left exposed to diquat dibromide.
requested_duration: 15 minutes to present, 5 minutes for Q&A

title: Elucidation of the Isoform and Role of SRSF1 in Simian Virus 40 T-antigen Transformed Human Diploid Fibroblasts
abstract: Cancer results from the accumulation of DNA mutations within one cell, resulting in the production of hyper- or non-functional proteins. Additionally, DNA can remain wild type and the resulting mRNA transcripts can be alternatively spliced to create proteins which contribute to tumorigenesis. To study the mechanisms by which tumor viruses induce this alternative splicing, our laboratory utilized the Simian Virus 40 (SV40) T-antigen oncoprotein. SV40 has been shown to cooperate with oncoproteins to promote transformation of human cells. To determine if alternative splicing plays a role in T-ag-transformation this project is investigated the splicing proteins SAM68 and SRSF1 in immortalized and transformed human diploid fibroblasts HDF(tert) and HDF(tert)+T, respectively. T-ag-transformed cells exhibited higher levels of the splicing factor SAM68. A target of SMA68 is SRSF1, which is also a splicing factor. SRSF1 is involved in pre-mRNA splicing and post-splicing activities like mRNA nuclear export and translation. SRSF1 contains two functional domains: an arginine-serine rich regulatory region, and two RNA-recognition-motifs. Three known SRSF1 isoforms are created by alternative splicing. SRSF1 retaining intron 4, has been shown to cause cells to transition from an epithelial-to-mesenchymal state (EMT) leading to a more aggressive and invasive tumor. It has been shown that SAM68 interacts with SRSF1 to allow for the inclusion of intron 4. This study aimed to use HDF(tert) and HDF(tert)+T to analyze the different SRSF1 isoforms and correlate that to the EMT. It was postulated that cells expressing higher levels of SAM68 will induce more SRSF1-containing intron 4 isoforms.
requested_duration: 15 minutes to present, 5 minutes for Q&A

title: How Positive Student-Professor Relationships Affect Academic Success and Motivation in Vulnerable College Students
abstract: How the quality of student-professor relationships affects students’ learning experience in college is given little attention. The current study explores how vulnerable college students’ relationships with professors affect their academic motivation and success. In particular, the groups were students of color, first-generation students, and first-year students. The study also examined whether students of color would have higher quality relationships with professors who were also people of color. Teacher-student relationship (TSR) quality, success, and motivation of these groups were compared to that of White students, continuing-generation students, and advanced students. The sample included students of all majors (N = 82; 73.3% women) who reported the quality of relationships with their professors, their academic motivation, and academic success. To determine quality of relationships, participants completed the Student Instructor-Relationship Scale (SIRS) for one current professor they got along well with and again for current professors in general. Participants also completed the Academic Motivation Scale – College Version (AMS-C 28) and provided their GPA as a measure of academic success. Results showed students of color, first-generation students, and first-year students did not have significantly different qualities of relationships with their professors compared to White students, non-first-generation students, and advanced students. Further, relationship quality between participants and their professors were not correlated with academic success and motivation. Lastly, student and faculty race was not related to relationship quality. To fully understand experiences of vulnerable college students and their relationships with professors, a more representative sample is needed in future research.
requested_duration: 15 minutes to present, 5 minutes for Q&A

title: Changing Ethnocultural Empathy in White Adults
abstract: This study examines the impact of watching an emotional narrative supporting the BLM movement from a Black individual on ethnocultural empathy while also assessing for color-blind attitudes and anti-racist behaviors in White adults. Research shows that color blindness (Mekawi et al., 2020; Neville et al., 2014) and ethnocultural empathy (Lu et al., 2020; Peifer et al., 2016; Wei et al., 2016) have powerful effects on multiculturalism attitudes. Color blindness refers to the idea of ignoring a person’s race, therefore discouraging discussion of racial differences and perpetuating existing inequalities (Hagerman, 2017; Perry et al., 2019; Vittrup, 2018; Underhill, 2018). Ethnocultural empathy develops through interactions with people who are different from ourselves (Godcharles et al., 2019; Lu et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2003) and refers to the ability to feel what someone of a different cultural background is feeling (Godcharles et al., 2019; Wei et al., 2016). It was hypothesized that there would be a greater difference in the pre- and post-ethnocultural empathy scores for those assigned to the emotional speaker condition compared to the research speaker condition.  	The hypothesis was supported; this study suggests that viewing a short, emotional stimulus can increase ethnocultural empathy for White adults (ages 18 – 80). It is unknown how long the increase in ethnocultural empathy lasts. Engaging with an emotional first-person narrative that relates to race may increase the ability to feel what someone of another cultural background is feeling. This may be a key step in decreasing racism among White people.
requested_duration: 15 minutes to present, 5 minutes for Q&A

title: It Takes a Village: How Perceived Social Support and Classroom Modality Impacts New Students’ Adjustments to College
abstract: COVID-19 has caused institutions across the world to operate at a hybrid or fully online level. This means that students who would typically begin their college career on campus, are now taking their classes on a computer without all of the typical college experiences. Brown (2001) found that new online students were less likely to feel like a part of their learning community than those who had taken online classes before. Lee, et al. (2020) explains that familial support is vital to a proper college transition and Bejerano (2014) adds that peer support is also important for a student’s adjustment to college life. During the 2020-2021 school year, the current study explored the impact of learning modality (in-person or online) on perceived social support and academic adjustment in first-year students at Elizabethtown College. The results suggest that online learners (M=35.69, SD=5.72) were not significantly different in academic adjustment than those who were considered in person learners (M=36.54, SD=6.4) t(79)=.447, p=.656. This is good news for Elizabethtown College, because it indicates that students feel they are still receiving a quality education, even in online courses. The results also suggest that in person students (M=5.73, SD=1.64) experienced more social support than online learners (M=4.98, SD=.94), t(85)=2.38, p=.02. Finally, the results support the hypothesis that a student’s level of perceived social support will relate to their academic adjustment. The correlation revealed a significant positive correlation between social support (M=5.61, SD=1.1, N=87) and academic adjustment (M=36.41, SD=6.27, N=81), r(79)=.415, p<.01.
requested_duration: 15 minutes to present, 5 minutes for Q&A

title: Social Media Trends: The Influence of Body Related Content on Body Image
abstract: In recent years, body related trends have become prevalent across various social media sites, however, their influence on body image remains unclear (Tiggermann & Zaccardo, 2015). The most common of these trends includes fitspiration, thinspiration, and body positivity. The present research examined the influence of these trends on various facets of body image such as body appreciation, body esteem, and body comparison. It was hypothesized that greater exposure to thinspiration and fitspiration, and greater exposure to general social media would negatively impact body image. Body positivity was hypothesized to have a positive impact on body image. The sample consisted of 40 participations, most being from Elizabethtown College. Participants first completed a baseline survey, which included questions related to demographics, general social media use, and body image variables. Through the use of Ecological Momentary Assessment (EMA), participants completed three daily surveys each day for one week. Daily survey questions were similar to those asked at baseline, but on a shorter scale. Results suggest that increased general social media use may negatively influence body appreciation. As hypothesized, greater exposure to thinspiration and fitspiration had an especially detrimental effect on body esteem. Body positivity had a significant positive impact on body appreciation. Future research should focus on gathering a larger, more representative sample in order to assess the true influence of these trends on body image.

title: Magic Squares
abstract: Magic squares are fun and relaxing mathematical puzzles made by arranging numbers 1 to n2  into an n by n grid where the sum in each row, column, and diagonals equal the same value. The oldest magic square is a 3-by-3 magic square mentioned in a Chinese book four to five thousand years before our era. Magic squares can be classified by the order n, or by the type of numbers used. In this presentation, we will share the history, some unique types of magic squares, and methods of forming magic squares.
requested_duration: 15 minutes to present, 5 minutes for Q&A

title: Sangaku Puzzles with GeoGebra
abstract: Sangaku, translated as ‘calculation tablet’ in Japanese, are Japanese geometrical problems on wooden tablets which were placed as offerings at Buddhist temples and Shinto shrines during the Edo period (1603-1868) by members are various social classes. During times of isolation from Western mathematical theory, Japanese mathematicians developed their own traditional mathematics. The problems typically featured geometric concepts such as mutually tangent circles or tangent spheres, circles inscribed in triangles, side and angle relations, and other visual geometric problems that display various principle theorems of mathematics. Over the ages, near 200 of these drawings and problems have survived the passage of time. In this project, Joseph and Allyson will solve ten or more of these problems and visualize their answers using the interactive geometric application GeoGebra. The results will be presented at SCAD.
requested_duration: 15 minutes to present, 5 minutes for Q&A

title: Sudoku And Methods to Solve Sudoku
abstract: Sudoku is a mathematical puzzle that exercises your brain and gives you a sense of accomplishment. The standard sudoku consists of a 9 by 9 grid containing 81 cells. The grid is subdivided into nine 3 by 3 blocks. Player fills numbers 1 through 9 into this 9 by 9 grid without repeating numbers in any row, column or block. Puzzle comes with some numbers already placed in some cells. In this presentation, we will talk about the origin of Sudoku, introduce various methods such as the Naked Singles method and compare strategies for solving this timeless puzzle.
requested_duration: 15 minutes to present, 5 minutes for Q&A

title: The Golden Ratio
abstract: The Golden Ratio, also known as Golden Section, Golden Mean, Divine Proportion, or the Greek letter Phi (?), is a special number that approximately equals 1.6180. The Golden Ratio can be found almost anywhere, like nature, architecture, painting, and music. We explore the history of this famous ratio, show the relation to Fibonacci’s sequence, and share solutions to some of many related mathematical problems.
requested_duration: 15 minutes to present, 5 minutes for Q&A

title: Marietta, Pennsylvania’s Historic Homes On Front Street: Transportation, Trade, Triumph, and Tragedy Along The Susquehanna River and the Pennsylvania Canal
abstract: The Maryland-based Chesapeake Bay Trust awarded Marietta Borough a $237,515 grant in 2021.  The funding is being used to improve a section of the Northwest Lancaster County River Trail running through Marietta.  A gravel section of trail will be replaced with porous pavement and lined with water-capturing rain gardens.  This public works project will make the trail complainant with the Americans with Disabilities Act.  This spring 2021 semester, students enrolled in Jean-Paul Benowitz’s course: Honors/Public Heritage Studies 201: Elizabethtown History: Campus and Community,” are conducting National Historic Preservation Act Section 106 Reviews about 17 historically significant properties along the trail. The students have researched the social, cultural, and economic relationship of historic properties along Front Street to transportation and trade along the Susquehanna River and the Pennsylvania Canal.  Students have plotted their findings on a ArcGIS map. This project relates to the Mellon Grant: “Confronting Challenges with Confidence: Humanities for Our World Today,” specifically regarding “Regional Heritage Studies.”  This project employs the active learning pedagogy from the National Collegiate Honors Council’s City as Text™.  The students’ scholarship is contributing to Marietta’s asset-based planning process to identify and mobilize existing as well as unrecognized resources such as physical, human, social, financial, environmental, political, cultural, and historical assets.  Students are implementing a “This Place Matters” campaign in Marietta.  This Place Matters is a national campaign, created by the National Historic Preservation Trust, encouraging people to celebrate places meaningful to them while inspiring an ongoing dialogue about the importance of place and preservation.
requested_duration: Poster

A gravel section of trail will be replaced with porous pavement and lined with water-capturing rain gardens.  This public works project will make the trail complainant with the Americans with Disabilities Act.  This spring 2021 semester, students enrolled in Jean-Paul Benowitz’s course: Honors/Public Heritage Studies 201: Elizabethtown History: Campus and Community,” are conducting National Historic Preservation Act Section 106 Reviews about 17 historically significant properties along the trail. The students have researched the social, cultural, and economic relationship of historic properties along Front Street to transportation and trade along the Susquehanna River and the Pennsylvania Canal.  Students have plotted their findings on a ArcGIS map. This project relates to the Mellon Grant: “Confronting Challenges with Confidence: Humanities for Our World Today,” specifically regarding “Regional Heritage Studies.”  This project employs the active learning pedagogy from the National Collegiate Honors Council’s City as Text™.  The students’ scholarship is contributing to Marietta’s asset-based planning process to identify and mobilize existing as well as unrecognized resources such as physical, human, social, financial, environmental, political, cultural, and historical assets.  Students are implementing a “This Place Matters” campaign in Marietta.  This Place Matters is a national campaign, created by the National Historic Preservation Trust, encouraging people to celebrate places meaningful to them while inspiring an ongoing dialogue about the importance of place and preservation.

title: Interoception Awareness and Intuitive Eating
abstract: Weight management changes throughout the lifespan and the transition to college is a time period when students need to nourish themselves independently. Weight management techniques include external mechanisms (calorie counting, point systems, etc.) and internal mechanisms (acknowledging hunger and satiety signals). The success of weight loss long term is a life long struggle for many, but internal mechanisms (i.e. Intuitive Eating) appears to have more success long term (Tribole et al., 2020).     Interoceptive awareness occurs when an individual processes, perceives, and tries to make meaning of an internal sensation (Tribole et al., 2020). When interoceptive awareness is cultivated, it is believed that people can be more in touch with the physical sensation of hunger (Tribole et al., 2020). If one cannot recognize hunger or satiety, is Intuitive Eating possible?     When interoception awareness, particularly of hunger and satiety are impaired, do individuals attempting to manage weight need to use external tools (such as MyFitness Pal, calorie counting, etc.)? For other students, they may have high interoceptive awareness, which means they do not need certain tools (e.g. calorie counting apps, portion sizing, etc.) to tell them when and what to eat, since they use their body signals to guide them. This study looked at a correlation between Interoception Awareness and weight management success using internal vs. external tools. The implications for the research lays the possible groundwork to consider using interventions to improve interoception awareness as part of a weight management program.
