title: Client perspectives of engaging in romantic relationships after a spinal cord injury: A phenomenological inquiry
abstract: Intimacy and romantic relationships are an integral component of an individual, providing love and support through one’s lifetime and increasing life satisfaction and well-being (Ferreira et al., 2014; Umberson & Montez, 2010). However, individuals who live with a spinal cord injury (SCI) experience relationships and intimacy differently than the rest of the population. Being paralyzed after any injury can affect the individual’s self-esteem, making the individual feel unattractive and self-conscious (Angel & Kroll, 2020; Fritz et al., 2015; Hwang et al., 2007). Current literature suggests a variety of client reported barriers to engaging in romantic relationships after SCI such as decreased self-esteem, negative body image, and lack of support and education; however, there is limited research regarding the lived experiences of individuals with SCI regarding intimacy (Angel & Kroll, 2020; Fritz et al., 2015; Hwang et al., 2007). Having a better understanding of the personal perspectives of individuals with SCI related to engaging in intimacy and romantic relationships will help occupational therapists to better address their clients’ needs after SCI. This study addressed the following research questions: 1) What are the personal experiences of individuals with SCI engaging in romantic relationships? 2) What are the reported facilitators and barriers of engaging in romantic relationships for individuals with SCI? And 3) How do individuals with SCI think that occupational therapy can better support their engagement in romantic relationships? This project was completed using a phenomenological approach and semi-structured interviews, which were transcribed and analyzed for common themes.

title: To Keep or Not to Keep: The Effects of Education and Political Ideology on Views of Abortion
abstract: The examination of public views of abortion has once again gained public attention due to the increase in restrictive legislative on abortion and the appointment of Supreme Court Justice Amy Coney Barret. In addition, the 2020 Reproductive Report card recently scored the United States with an F largely due to abortion services and availability or the lack thereof. Previous literature found a relationship between political ideology, education level, and abortion views. This research examines the effects of education and political ideology on views of abortion controlling for sex using data obtained from the 2018 wave of the General Social Survey (GSS) conducted by the National Opinion Research Center (NORC) at the University of Chicago. After deleting missing cases, the total sample size was 523. Preliminary results showed greater support for abortions categorized as hard compared to views of abortions categorized as soft. Additional bivariate and multivariate results will be presented.

title: Conflict Resolution and Sociology: An Ethnographic Analysis
abstract: Sociology permeates nearly every field that interacts with institutional structures, cultures, and group behaviors. During my semester long internship with Advoz, a community organization based in Mediation and Restorative Practices, I have found a strong intersection between the conflict resolution field and sociology. Culture, religion, and race are present during conflict and without a foundational understanding of structures and social dynamics, resolution can be unsuccessful. Through participant observation and semi-structured interviews with Advoz staff members, I have found that a background in sociology is important (and perhaps even necessary) for conflict resolution work. In this presentation, I will explain the sociological imagination as envisioned by C. Wright Mills in 1959 and discuss the benefits of applying the sociological imagination to conflict resolution.

title: Is the UN an Effective Peacekeeper?: A Comparative Analysis of Peacekeeping Missions in Rwanda and Liberia
abstract: Since it is establishment, The UN has been an organization dedicated to keeping peace around the world. However, despite its goals the UN has both failed and succeeded in many different peacekeeping missions. This paper will attempt to answer the question of what makes peacekeeping successful and come up with suggestions about how peacekeeping can be improved. The thesis of this paper is that the success of UN peacekeeping missions depends on the flexibility of its mandate, the amount of support given by countries to the UN, and consensus in the security council during the mission. This paper will be a focused comparison, in that it will compare both UN involvement in Rwanda and Liberia. Rwanda is considered to be an unsuccessful example of UN peacekeeping, while many consider Liberia to be a success. The paper will analyze the history of both missions and discuss in detail both the achievements and shortcomings of each respectfully. The conclusion of this paper supports the original thesis and discusses changes to the UN can may help future peacekeeping missions.

title: The Age of Climate Change
abstract: The Paris Climate Accord was the first global commitment to tackle climate change. Even though the agreement's effectiveness has been debated amongst scholars, almost every country in the world has signed it. This paper examines the relative effects of constitutional, economic, and political factors on the progress that signatories to the Paris Climate Accord have made in reaching their agreed-upon targets. Through the use of crosstabulations, correlations, and multivariate analysis, the statistical analysis of data showed that countries that are considered democracies, have a constitutional provision on the environment, and are developed economies are doing better at meeting the goals of the Paris Climate Accord.

title: Outdated Laws: Their Contributions to Mass Incarceration and Police Practices
abstract: This paper will examine two major federal laws: the Anti-Drug Act of 1989 and the 1994 Crime Bill. It will provide context to two current problems the United States is dealing with: mass incarceration and controversial police practices. By analyzing these laws, we will be able to see a direct correlation between outdated laws, and the way policing has been impacted. The laws are not up-to-date with modern societal views, leading to a push for massive criminal justice reform.

title: The Latinx Vote: The Cuban American Vote Explained
abstract: This paper's primary purpose is to explore the different characteristics of the Latinx vote, its development throughout the years, and how divided it is. It will examine why most Cuban Americans residing in the United States identify politically as Republicans. Furthermore, this paper aims to explore the reasoning behind second and third generations of Cuban Americans developing a more liberal ideology and how this defies their ancestors' ideologies. Finally, I will explore why new generations of Cubans arriving in the U.S. have a less belligerent vision of commitment to the Cuban people and even of consent to the opening of diplomatic relations between the U.S. and Cuba.

title: DuBois and Associates - A Family Business Case Study
abstract: The paper presents the story of an actual family business, developed as a case study with recommendations and creative solutions. The research is aimed to describe and assess the company, identify the most important challenges faced by the family firm, and develop recommendations on how to solve these issues. The paper involves both primary research - in-depth interviews with family members, managers, and owners and other data collection methods, and secondary research - literature review and industry reports.

title: Tackling the Hikikomori Issue in Japan: Open Dialogue is the Best Method
abstract: Hikikomori are people in Japan with no pre-existing mental conditions who are socially withdrawn and stay inside their house for more than six months. They do not communicate with other people except with their family members. In this document, I will be explaining the research history of Hikikomori, why this issue has become so prevalent in Japan, and comparing it with the cultures of other countries. I will be explaining why the open dialogue method is the best method for treating Hikikomori. After summarizing the research history and presenting statistical data, I will be examining Japanese culture and comparing and contrasting with other countries. I will be documenting different cases of Hikikomori in Japan to show why this issue is serious and what solutions can help solve the issue. The argument is that the open dialogue method is the best method for treating Hikikomori.

title: Macbeth and Throne of Blood: The Allure of Power
abstract: Shakespeare’s Macbeth is one of the most well-known and well-regarded works of fiction ever created. Since it was written in 1606, there have been countless adaptations and interpretations of Shakespeare’s play about Medieval Scotland. One such adaptation is Akira Kurosawa’s Throne of Blood, which had the basic plot and character roles of Macbeth, but the character names were changed as well as the setting to fit Sengoku period Japan. This film, and perhaps the play it was adapting, have much to say about the nature of power and ambition. In fact, the beginning of Throne of Blood literally states outright that the main character was killed by his own ambition. However, both of these works have different ways of going about their morals. Macbeth ends with a western moral of a just political force coming to set things right, but Throne of Blood reinterprets that ending to show that even the political force that kills the main character is motivated by their own agenda. It is through these works that this paper will analyze the similarities and differences between the works themselves, as well as the time periods of their respective settings, in order to understand what attracts people to power and the nature of ambition. The questions asked are “Why do people want power?”, “What is the allure of ambition?”, and “How can power, or even the allure of power, corrupt?” Using Throne of Blood and Macbeth, this paper will compare and contrast Sengoku Period Japan and Medieval Scotland.

title: Playing with Dolls: The Difference of Artistic Value Between Bunraku and Puppet Shows
abstract: From preschool productions of classic fairytales to the modern-day playhouses of Japan’s elite, puppets have played a larger role in cultures across the globe than most people would expect.  When most people in America think of puppets, their first thoughts are of Jim Henson’s Muppets or Joan Ganz Cooney’s Sesame Street.  On the other hand, when people in Japan hear the word ningyo, they think of Uemura Bunrakuken’s bunraku with handcrafted, artisan made dolls that are brought to life on the stage by three master handlers.  But what separates brown paper bag puppets from the wooden ningyo of bunraku in terms of artistic merit?  Why are puppet shows considered a childish form of media entertainment while ningyo joruri performances are considered a traditional form of art worthy of high respect?  Why are puppets used with solely comedic purpose in mind while ningyo are used to tell stories rife with drama and intrigue?  Where do the two forms of art overlap and how did they evolve into the media forms they are in the modern world?  The aim of this paper, then, is to examine the differences between the performances, puppets, and target audiences of puppet shows and bunraku.  To do this, we will look through the lens of historical examination to determine how the respective art forms evolved throughout time and what this evolution tells us about the values, histories, and cultures of American and Japanese societies in which these performances thrive.

title: Protesting in France and the US
abstract: In this presentation I will summarize modern protest movements in France and the US and investigate how societal constructs and social media have revolutionized manifestations in the 2010s and beyond. The individualism that drives both capitalism and the American dream contrasts directly with France’s emphasis on strong union. Furthermore, the United State’s federalized system makes a united front hard to achieve while France’s centralized government thrives of uniformity. Striking in France has been a proven tool to gain workers rights, while in the US, from the civil rights movements of the 1960s to the modern day Black Lives Matter protests there is a long history of protesting as well. Using recent protests and shifting demographics as tools, I hope to examine how protesting is taking place in each country in the last decade. I will also examine the ways in which social media and globalization are altering the art of the protest. Protesting is a constant in every society and with the rise of social media it is becoming a shared experience for us all.

title: Associations Among Music Selections, Emotion Words, and Color for Six Emotions
abstract: Limited research has been conducted on the relationship among all three variables: music, emotions, and colors (Palmer et al., 2016). Therefore, this study sought to investigate if the rating scores that associated six colors with each of six emotions differed depending on whether the method for conveying the emotion was a feeling word expressing the emotion or a short music selection expressing the emotion. Following IRB approval, we asked 91 participants to complete a three-part survey in which they: a) rated how 12 musical selections, two for each of 6 emotions (happy, sad, angry, scared, calm, and proud) were associated with six colors (red, orange, yellow, green, blue and purple); b) rated how six emotion words were associated with the six colors; and c) identified how they made their decisions. Following a significant three-way interaction (music x word x color), the results suggested that while a similar pattern of association existed for word and music expressions for the more commonly used emotions (sad with blue, happy with yellow, and angry with red), the pattern of associations for word and music expressions differed across less commonly used emotions, calm, proud, and scared. Music therapists may find using colors as a visual input modality or an icon medium for emotional expression along with music may provide another resource for better understanding clients’ nonverbal expressions. However, while agreement was obtained for some emotions, caution also must be used for other emotions in which associations are more individualized.

title: The Mighty Handful and the Development of the Russian Sound
abstract: Russian national music was developed in the late nineteenth century by a group of composers called the Mighty Handful. This group consisted of five composers named Balakirev, Borodin, Mussorgsky, Rimsky-Korsakov, and Cui. They were inspired by the literary movement of realism as well as previous composers in both the Nationalist and cosmopolitan styles. This along with various musical elements including harmonizations, a better Russian declamation, and the implementation of elements of folk music, led to Russian Nationalist music.  	The Mighty Handful was formed in the 1860s and 1870s. The members were all involved in the musical life of St. Petersburg, even though few of them were professional musicians. Balakirev acted as the leader of the group and sought to continue the work of a composer named Glinka in incorporating folk elements into Russian music. The group used musical elements such as unusual scales, modal harmonizations, and different textures to create the Russian sound. They also incorporated a more faithful declamation style in the Russian language, the literary movement toward realism, and changes to the perception of time in their music. Through these elements, they created music that sounded distinctly Russian. This paper will introduce and explain many of the stylistic innovations the Mighty Handful used.

title: The Developing Salience Network of Babies with Neonatal Abstinence Syndrome and Music Therapy Protocol
The Developing Salience Network of Babies with Neonatal Abstinence Syndrome and Music Therapy Protocol
abstract: The recent drug epidemic continues to not only place mothers at risk but also their infants born dependent on those drugs (Sanlorenzo et al., 2018). When exposed in utero to addictive drugs taken by the mother, infants are often born with Neonatal Abstinence Syndrome (NAS). While more recent research on the neurobiology of music and the brain supports the benefits of current music therapy treatments, the salience network (SN) also may provide additional insight into the effects of music with babies with NAS. Therefore, this research project seeks to gain an understanding of the benefits of current music therapy protocol from two perspectives: a) a review of the neuroscience literature on the SN and its impact on babies with NAS, and b) an analysis of two interviews with music therapists working with infants diagnosed with NAS. Following IRB approval, 15 fact-based and 15 concept-oriented interview questions will be asked of two music therapists, analyzed for common themes, and compared to the results from the literature. The review of literature found that a network related to the SN begins to develop just before birth (Alcauster et al., 2014) and is negatively impacted by drug addiction (Zilverstand et al., 2018). The interview questions will solicit information about the timing of treatment, protocol implemented, and usage of neuroscience in practice. The researcher hypotheses that current treatment generally supports the needs of the developing salience network; however, addition neuroscience training could further enhance the implementation treatment protocol.

title: Convergence of art and science in Anatomy and Physiology course; the student perspective
abstract: Integration of arts and humanities into the science curriculum can help train healthcare workers develop emotional intelligence, empathy, and communication skills. These “soft” skills can give medical professionals the tools to help patients from diverse backgrounds with various physical and emotional needs. We discuss ways in which we incorporate arts into the Human Anatomy and Physiology course through creative extra credit assignments to empower students to apply course content by developing community outreach, art exhibits, and education events.  We will also present data reflecting student perspective on the educational value of these assignments.

title: Effects on Bacterial Composition from Long-term Storage of Fecal Matter
abstract: Fecal Matter Transplantation (FMT) is an innovative treatment that has in clinical trials, resolved 80-90% of infections caused by the recurrent Clostridium difficile bacterium which does not respond to antibiotics. During FMT, a fecal preparation from a healthy stool donor is transplanted into the colon of the patient. Stool banks, such as OpenBiome, store donor stool samples at their biorepository facilities, for a maximum of two years. However, there lack studies examining the bacterial composition, for such long-term storage, for fecal matter. Therefore, this study aimed to compare the effects of long-term storage on the composition of microbes using fecal matter obtained from dogs. To study long term effects, stored fecal matter samples were analyzed after five months, one year, and three years of storage in a deionized water with 25% glycerol solution at -80 °C. Community DNA was extracted from the original samples for analysis. After DNA extraction, the V4 region of DNA was amplified using PCR and sent for sequencing. Data were analyzed for changes in microbial composition across time using the Qiime software. Preliminary analysis of the data suggests the greatest change occurs when the stool sample is first stored.  For a more comprehensive answer, further analyses will be conducted. The results from this study will provide greater insight towards the maximum storage period suitable for greatest bacterial recovery. Additionally, results could provide better understanding towards methods for bacterial storage intended for Fecal Matter Transplant.

title: Menthol’s Impact on Environmental Cues When Used in Combination with Nicotine
abstract: Nicotine is a nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (nAChR) agonist that increases dopamine (DA) firing in the ventral tegmental area (VTA) causing increased DA levels in the nucleus accumbens (NAc). Menthol is a flavorant commonly used in tobacco products to mask the aversive taste of nicotine and relieve irritation from smoke inhalation. Menthol is well known to exacerbate tobacco addiction.  I will be discussing the data from two separate studies and relating them back to each other. I analyzed behavioral neuroscience data collected from rats for my neuroscience thesis and conducted and analyzed data on smoking behavior through the use of a psychological survey for my psychology thesis.  The first study used fast scan cyclic voltammetry to examine the effects of nicotine and menthol, intraperitoneally administered alone and in combination, on phasic dopamine release in the nucleus accumbens of male Sprague-Dawley rats. Results confirmed that nicotine, but not menthol, enhances phasic dopamine release in the nucleus accumbens. Acute menthol added to nicotine did not enhance phasic dopamine release above that elicited by nicotine.  The second study used an online survey to collect data on the smoking preferences of smokers over the age of 18 to examine the behavioral differences between menthol and nonmenthol smokers. Data is currently being collected and has not yet been analyzed, however full analyses will be conducted, and results will be discussed and related back to study one.

title: Effect of Juror Perceptions of the Insanity Defense and Mental Illness within the Criminal Justice System
abstract: This study examined the relationship between bias against defendants pleading “not guilty by reason of insanity” (NGRI) and those labeled as a psychopath during trial. It also examined potential relationships between conservative values, authoritarian views, or attitudes towards the insanity defense and how these relate to acceptance of a NGRI plea. Eighty-two college students ages 18 - 25 completed a within-subjects experiment consisting of four different conditions, two with defendants labeled as psychopaths, and two without, and two with NGRI pleas and two without. Participants also answered case evaluation questions about each condition and completed survey questions from the Revised Insanity Defense Attitudes Scale (IDA-R), the Authoritarian subscale of the Revised Legal Attitudes Questionnaire (R-LAQ-A), and the Conservatism Scale.  Results indicate that attitudes about the insanity defense and strict liability of the defendant did impact the answers that participants gave throughout the evaluation questions, most noticeably when the NGRI plea was present in the vignette. Furthermore, scores on the conservatism scale and the R-LAQ-A exhibited the strongest relationship with participant scores on the case evaluation questions where “psychopath” was utilized within the vignette. This reveals a relationship where stronger negative views towards this label were seen in participants who held greater conservative and authoritarian views.

title: Effects of Catastrophes on Insurance and Reinsurance Markets
abstract: In recent years, there has been an uptick in catastrophe losses in the United States. In 2020 alone, some major catastrophes included Hurricane Laura, the Western wildfires, and of course the Coronavirus pandemic.   In my senior thesis presentation, I plan to explore the effects of catastrophes on the insurance and reinsurance markets. I will talk about the measures, such as reinsurance and catastrophe bonds, that are taken to prepare for possible catastrophic losses. In addition, I plan to discuss several different factors that effect reinsurance, including moral hazard and adverse selection, and consider the possibility that not even reinsurance is enough to handle certain risks.  	My plan is to spend a good portion of the presentation focusing on pandemics and Covid-19. I will talk about the main effects of the Coronavirus pandemic on insurance companies, specifically in the health insurance sector since that is the sector I will be pursuing after college. I will also look at whether insurance companies were able to adapt during the pandemic to stay afloat.   	Another important piece of my presentation is to discuss the different models that are being built to predict catastrophic losses. I will comment on how these models are being built, look at the assumptions underlying the models, and dive into their mathematical nature a bit.   	Finally, I will look to the future and discuss what insurance and reinsurance markets are doing to better prepare for future catastrophes.

title: The Rise of the Machine: How Industrial Robots Will Revolutionize U.S. Manufacturing
abstract: The purpose of the project is to outline the historical developments of robotics and automation, the current state of the field, and potential future outcomes of how robotics can be applied for the betterment of humankind. The presentation will focus on key areas of the historical movements that led up to this point, such as scientific management, as well as depictions of robotics and automation in popular culture. Popular misconceptions of the function and integration of robots and automation into daily life will be dispelled, and a particular focus will be put on how they should be implemented into economic systems to augment human workers instead of replacing them.    I will also host a discussion about modular robotics, and how their potential usage would be the most useful to future automation efforts instead of putting a focus on the hyper-specialized robots that are common in industrial automation today. Examples based on the Arduino platform will be used for the purposes of the presentation.

title: PIKA: A Real-life PokéDex on a Smartphone with the Power of Deep Learning
abstract: Image classification is a popular topic in the world of machine learning and deep learning. Now that almost every individual in America carries a smartphone in their pocket, new technologies have emerged to take advantage of this power. There exists a large variety of unexplored applications and use cases for deep learning, and PIKA attempts to expand the realm of what is possible with image classification. The well-known show Pokémon introduces numerous new creatures who must be classified in the show by a device known as the PokéDex. Within the project, PIKA, we explore how deep learning can be utilized to identify these creatures with high accuracy, just like in the fictional world of Pokémon. The project leverages emerging repositories to achieve all this, such as Keras from Tensorflow which is used for creating deep learning models, and Kivy to create the main phone app and layout.

title: Standing, Sharing, and Scrolling: How In-Person Protesting and Social Media Activism Impact Social Connectedness to Local Community
abstract: Social life has undisputedly changed since March 2020. Social distancing and interaction mandates to contain COVID-19 changed how individuals and communities connect. At the same time, due to social unrest and contested political terrain, civic engagement increased. Previous research states political activism and neighborhood activism improved well-being. Additionally, prior studies found that social media has potential to increase connectedness; however, the direct effects are unclear. This Honors in the Discipline in Sociology research used survey methodology to explore the relationship between civic engagement, in-person protesting, and social media activism on feelings of connectedness to the community in Central Pennsylvania. Preliminary results will be presented.

title: To Vote or Not to Vote: The Effects of Political Information Efficacy, Locus of Control, and Parental Socialization on the Political Engagement of College Students
abstract: Political engagement involves both indirect and direct actions that effect the political system such as voting, donating to campaigns, and volunteering for a political party. Previous literature has suggested that students demonstrating more interest in politics and exhibiting strong party ties were more likely to vote than those who were uninterested in politics. Limited research has examined the relationship between political information efficacy, locus of control, and parental socialization on the political engagement of college students; however, studies have thoroughly examined the effects of political affiliation. Self-efficacy, locus of control, and the social learning theory were used to analyze the relationship between political information efficacy, locus of control, and parental socialization on the political engagement of traditional age college students from a sociological perspective. The sample population for this research were students enrolled at one small, private, liberal arts institution located in central Pennsylvania. The data were obtained through the use of mixed methodology, using survey and semi-structured interview techniques. The preliminary findings from this Honors in the Discipline in Sociology research will be presented.

title: That’s News to Me: A Content Analysis of the Portrayal of Perpetrators of Mass Murder in Mass Media Communications
abstract: The United States holds only five percent of the world’s population, but surprisingly 31 percent of global mass shootings. Previous literature defines a mass shooting as an incident where at least four individuals are shot and a mass murder as an incident where at least four individuals are killed. Mass shootings have been found to occur in bunches due to the exposure of mass shootings inspiring copycat shootings. Such inspiration has been potentially linked to media coverage of these events thus giving them “accidental advertising”. Limited research has empirically examined the news coverage of mass shootings through a content analysis. This exploratory research used quantitative and thematic content analysis to examine two qualitatively different mass shootings, the Las Vegas Concert shooting and the Dayton Nightclub shooting, and the news coverage of each event. The data for this research were obtained from a content analysis of articles from a local Las Vegas news website, The Las Vegas Sun, a local Dayton, OH news website, The Dayton Daily News, and AP News. Results will be presented and compared to the proposed guidelines for the coverage of mass shootings by media organizations.

title: Revoking Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act
abstract: The purpose of my presentation is to give the average internet user an inside look at Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act, and the massive implications it will have for American lives if it is revoked. My research topic is very timely, considering calls for revocation by current President Joe Biden and former President Donald Trump. I will analyze the different perspectives and approaches, including international affairs, to revoking Section 230. Along the way, I will examine why social media became an unregulated organ for political disinformation, and how the United States government failed to counter it with legislative action. Calls for reform by Republicans were provoked by perceived liberal bias of major social media platforms. Democrats' concerns picked up in 2020 due to a rise in violence and foreign actors using social media as a propaganda weapon to interfere in United States elections. Calls have gotten even louder since the 2021 storming of the United States Capitol. Finally, the paper will tackle the consequences and drawbacks of revoking Section 230.

title: Modern Reparations for African-Americans
abstract: Since May of last year, racial tensions have surged. Sparked by the death of George Floyd at the hands of police officers, protests for racial equality raged across the country all summer and into the fall. In response, many organizations, including the government, considered ways in which they could help advance racial equality. However, true racial equality and equity cannot be met until past injustices have been atoned for.  Centuries of racism and discrimination have had traumatic effects on the Black community. The most influential of these is a massive wealth gap between white and Black families; today, the average white family has ten times the wealth of the average black family. To achieve a racially equal and equitable society, reparations in the forms of education, business, and housing investment for the Black community are needed to close the wealth gap.

title: The Professionalization of a Family Business
abstract: To achieve sustainable business and family relationships, family firms should transition toward formal structures and processes as growth and succession occur. In this research project, we explore what types of professionalization processes are necessary for a family business growth and continuity. Topics such as the introduction of professional management, the formalization of the family business across its organizational life cycle, and the best practices of professionalization are investigated. The findings serve to make recommendations to a family business on how to develop and implement a professionalization strategy.

title: Improving Family Business Governance by Designing Effective Boards
abstract: Despite of the important role and potential of family businesses, there are many challenges that need to be addressed in order to keep them afloat. One of these challenges is the family boards and governance.  The vast majority of family firms are reluctant to address this topic. The family business boards play a huge role in guiding family firms toward renewal and continuity.  However, for some families this is a struggle because of various family, ownership, and management conflicts. Moreover, some businesses do not have a board or other governance structures at all. The paper investigates key family business governance processes and, from a practitioner’s perspective, proposes measures to develop and strengthen their corporate governance.

title: Family Businesses Resilience to Crises
abstract: Understanding the uniqueness of family businesses requires the investigation of their capacity to withstand crises, including the current economic crisis triggered by the COVID-19 pandemic. Family businesses have proved a higher resilience both pre and post economic crisis, compared with non-family businesses. They are better equipped to deal with economic challenges, return to growth faster, and continue to record higher returns over time. The paper investigates some of the best practices of dealing with the current crisis and makes recommendations to a family business on various strategies to ensure growth and continuity.

title: Designing the Transition of a Family Business to the Next Generation
abstract: Succession planning is crucial to the success and continuity of any business. For a family business succession is particularly important as few survive more than one generation. Based on literature review, the paper analyses the key succession processes from the perspectives of both leadership and ownership transitions. Specific succession recommendations are developed for a family business.

title: Poetry as Resistance: People Power in Prose
abstract: As part of a supplemental honors assignment for IC 204: Artistic Peacebuilding, this essay will explore the history and significance of poetry as a form of sociopolitical resistance. This research will encompass not only the origins of poetry as a means of communicating political dissent, but it will highlight the role of poetry as it related to the autonomous expression of marginalized subcultures. Over the course of this essay, the following subjects will be explored: anti-war poetry and fatalism following WWI, poetry exploring the realities of racism and racial oppression, the role of underground poetry zines in the formation of queer communities, and the contemporary role of poetry in giving voice to the experiences of those living through violence. As a means of incorporating this contemporary perspective, the essay will feature an interview with poet and scholar Dr. Patricia Jabbeh Wesley. This interview will reference Wesley’s body of work regarding her experience living through the Liberian Civil War. The essay as a whole will explore the significance of poetry as a personal and vulnerable act of resistance and community-building.

title: The Book of Exodus in Film: A Story (Re)shaped by History
abstract: The story of the Exodus, Moses, and the Ten Commandments found in both the Christian and Hebrew Bible has received multiple film adaptations over the last 100+ years of American cinema. Each adaptation is able to present the story in a different way, and are particularly influenced by the time period of their release. Specifically, the adaptations of the Exodus present takeaways to the audience that reflect the ideas of the time period. Through the examination of the four major American film adaptations: The Ten Commandments (1923), The Ten Commandments (1956), The Prince of Egypt (1998), and Exodus: Gods and Kings (2014), the modern viewer can ultimately recognize the differing goals of each film and how they have shaped the overall understanding of The Book of Exodus in the shared cultural consciousness.

title: The Climate Crisis: What We Can Learn from Latin American Indigenous Groups
abstract: Climate change is a global problem that impacts all of the world. The majority of countries recognize the presence of climate change and admit, as a global community, we need to take action to slow the progression of global warming. Almost all of the countries in the world have a common goal in regard to climate change; however, as a global community we have not made the necessary changes in order to create positive change and achieve the goals outlined in the Paris Agreement. Even countries with great wealth are not on track to meet the goals outlined in the Paris Agreement. However, one can learn a lot from the practices and cultures of indigenous groups in Latin America. Many indigenous groups have devotion and respect for the Earth that is not present in the Western world. Through a literary analysis, the first half of the report discusses climate change and the Paris Agreement in a global manner, as well as the practices specific to Latin America. The second half offers an alternative to the conversation of climate change by discussing the practices and culture of the following indigenous groups: The Quechua people of Bolivia, the Wampis Nation of Peru, the Wiwa people of Colombia, and the Waorani people of Ecuador. Cultural differences are discussed, as well as suggestions of change for the western world from the perspective of various Latin American indigenous groups. This presentation will be given in Spanish.

title: Synthesis of Modified Amide-based Extended Heterocyclic Nucleobases Capable of Hydrogen Bonding to the U-A Base Pair in Double Stranded RNA
abstract: With the development of CRISPR-Cas9 and concerns with emerging pathogens such as the SARS-CoV-2 virus, RNA research has become increasingly important. Additionally, there is a growing interest in non-coding RNA which plays a role in catalyzing chemical reactions, regulating gene expression, and governing post-transcriptional modification. RNA’s tertiary structure contains many double helical regions which are prime for recognition by triplex forming oligonucleotides (TFOs). Peptide nucleic acid (PNA) has been utilized as a TFO to sequence selectively identify double stranded RNA (dsRNA). However, selectivity is limited to polypurine strands due to limited hydrogen bonding capability. Our work aims to afford better binding to the U-A base pair through extended aromatic systems. The Io series of nucleobases were designed to yield a third hydrogen bond, affording increased binding affinity and selectivity. However, recent data from these nucleobases suggests other factors including pi-stacking may be more prevalent in triplex formation. Herein we report the development of the synthesis of the Iop series, nucleobases analogous to Io series, without the third hydrogen bonding capability, allowing for comparisons between the importance of pi-stacking and hydrogen bonding in triplex formation.     We gratefully acknowledge the National Science Foundation (CHE – 1708699) and the Elizabethtown College Scholarship, Creative Arts, and Research Projects (SCARP) program for financial support.

title: Development of a Microwave Assisted One-Pot Allylation and Claisen Rearrangement
abstract: The Aromatic Claisen rearrangement is a widely applicable organic reaction that involves the shift of a sigma bond across the pi-system of an allyl phenol to produce ortho-allylated phenols. In this project, we have developed a microwave assisted allylation of phenols, followed by a subsequent Claisen rearrangement in one pot. Acetaminophen was chosen as a model phenol to test this chemistry. We aim to design and optimize a one-pot reaction that affords the highest yield of rearranged acetaminophen from the corresponding phenol. The optimization of the reaction includes conditions such as time, temperature, solvent, reagents, and stoichiometric equivalences. To date, the time, temperature, solvent, reagents, and work-up conditions have been explored. Current optimization work is focused on stoichiometry, the use of other reagents, and the development of an efficient LCMS method for accelerated determination of reaction mixtures. We have developed reaction conditions to obtain greater than 70% yield of isolated rearranged product. As a result, we have been able to further optimize the reaction to afford yields of rearranged acetaminophen, with the goal of exploring alternative phenols.

title: pH Sensitive Polymer Nanoparticle Control for a Lateral Flow Assay for Lead(II) Detection
abstract: Throughout the United States, more than two million people do not have access to clean water.  One of the main water contaminants is lead.  While it is possible to send a water sample to the lab to determine if heavy metals are present, this is expensive, time consuming, and requires trained personnel for instrument operation.  The goal of this research is to design an inexpensive testing method, based on a lateral flow assay, that allows people to test for heavy metals in their water while in their home.  The assay is designed so there are two lines that appear on the test strip: a control line which ensures the test is working properly, and a test line responsible for detecting metals present in the water.   In this work, we focused on developing polymer nanoparticles encapsulating the compound bromocresol green, which will constitute the control line and produce a signal at neutral pH.  The resulting nanoparticles were characterized through a variety of methods including DLS, zeta potential, and UV-Vis spectroscopy.  Incorporation of the nanoparticles into the lateral flow assay was performed through a streptavidin and biotin interaction.  When in acidic conditions, the synthesized nanoparticles bound to the test strip, demonstrating these nanoparticles can be used as the control in our assay.  At a basic pH, the opposite result was observed.  Future work aims to increase the stability of the control signal by testing nanoparticles encapsulating bromocresol purple, and also synthesizing nanoparticles from block polymers with various component ratios and molecular weights.

title: The effect of poly(I:C) on the immune system as observed through IL-12 production in dendritic cells
abstract: Activation of dendritic cells (DCs) through chemical treatment causes release of cytokines. Original studies demonstrated that MuTu DCs, derived from the spleen of mice, responded to stimulation of TLR3 with poly(I:C) by producing IL-12. Challenges in culture of MuTu DCs led to the transition to culture of the DC2.4 cell line. DC2.4 cells are also murine dendritic cells but derived from the bone marrow. Both DC lines express TLR3. To compare the response of DC2.4 cells to MuTu DCs, studies using varying doses and times of poly(I:C) exposure were conducted. In contrast to MuTu DCs, DC2.4 cells produced little to no IL-12 after 12-hour exposure to doses less than 5 µg/mL poly(I:C). Additional experiments determined what dose of poly(I:C) and exposure time was required to stimulate DC2.4 to produce larger amounts of IL-12. Other ongoing studies are investigating whether corticosterone (CORT) alters IL-12 production by DC2.4. CORT is a stress hormone known to suppress IL-12 production by MuTu DCs. Following activation, DCs often undergo programmed cell death, or apoptosis. This occurred when MuTu DCs were stimulated with poly(I:C). Bim, a member of the Bcl-2 family of proteins, promotes apoptosis, which can be triggered through administration of chemicals such as poly(I:C). Bim was successfully detected in Human Diploid Fibroblasts (HDF), which will serve as a positive control to optimize Bim detection in DCs. Analysis of the production of IL-12 by DCs and their subsequent apoptosis allows for greater understanding of how stress-induced chemicals affect our ability to fight pathogens.

title: Methods of Analyzing Taste Preference Reveal Menthol’s Ability to Drive Nicotine Consumption
abstract: Flavored tobacco products are widely popular, suggesting that taste may play a critical role in tobacco use. Evaluating how the addition of flavorants to oral tobacco products influences consumption is necessary to understanding how such flavorants drive nicotine use and addiction. Taste preference, in the context of oral nicotine consumption, has been previously investigated in various experimental paradigms. However, there is variability among existing literature on the best method of analyzing and presenting this measure. In the present investigation, we developed a series of two-bottle choice tests to evaluate taste preference in rats, comparing nicotine alone to nicotine solutions flavored with saccharine or menthol. We also compared several methods of analyses for taste preference (% preference, difference score, and taste index) in order to determine which offered the most valid and sensitive assessment of preference. The results of the analysis revealed that oral consumption of nicotine, on its own, is aversive. It was initially expected that the inherently appetitive flavorant, saccharine, would serve to increase preference. We did not find significant effects for the saccharine group, which may be attributed to the high concentration of nicotine used. Mentholated solutions, however, were found to be significantly preferred across all measures, suggesting that menthol may be a superior masker of nicotine’s aversive taste. Additionally, it was found that % preference and taste index offered identical results and provided the most sensitive measure of preference among those that were tested, indicating the importance of which assessment tool is utilized to evaluate taste preference.
